sections.overview:
Gokshura, Puncture Vine ( Tribulus terrestris / Tribulus alatus Del.) – Uses, Benefits, Ayurvedic Properties & Effects on Dosha 

 Gokshura Plant 
 Gokshura is a small, prostrate, hirsute or silky hairy herb. Gokshura leaves are stipulate, opposite, usually unequal, pinnate, leaflets 5-8 pairs, oblong, mucronate. Gokshura flowers are solitary, axillary or leaf opposed, yellow or white. Gokshura fruits are globose, hairy, 5-angled, and spinous with two long and two short spines on each cocci and Gokshura seeds are obliquely pendulous.

sections.reference:
The Bhavprakash nighantu with elaborated Hindi commentary by Padmashri prof. K.C. Chunekar, edited by Dr. G.S. Pandey: edition of 1998: verse 44-46, page no-292-293. 

 Special Note 
 Bhavamishra (a classical Ayurvedic scholar and author of Bhavprakash) describes only one variety of Gokṣura (a medicinal plant traditionally used for urinary and reproductive disorders). Another well-known variety, called Brihad Gokshura (meaning “large Gokshura”), is botanically identified as Pedalium murex Linn. This plant is also referred to as Shringarika in classical Samhitas (authoritative Ayurvedic texts). Shringarika is considered a variety of Laghu Singhada or Shringi, both names indicating plants with horn-like or spiny fruits. 
One of the synonyms of Gokshura is Trikantaka, which literally means “three-spined,” referring to the morphology of the fruit. However, this feature does not uniformly apply to both types of Gokshura. In Laghu Gokshura (small Gokshura), each fruit segment has two prominent spines; when the remaining minor spines are counted collectively as one, the description of three spines can be justified. Based on the term Trikantaka, Acanthospermum hispidum DC. has also been proposed by scholars, although this plant also lacks clearly defined three spines. 
In classical Ayurvedic literature, Shvadmshtra—meaning “dog’s tooth” due to the tooth-like spines of the plant—is mentioned more frequently than Gokshura, although Bhavmishra considers both to be synonymous. On this basis, Singh and Chunekar suggest identifying Shvadmshtra with Smilax aspera Linn. In local usage, it is known as Kukkurdadha, which also translates to “dog’s tooth” and is synonymous with Shvadmshtra. This plant is traditionally used as a Raktashodhaka (blood purifier). Therefore, Shvadmshtra may be regarded as an independent medicinal substance rather than merely a synonym of Gokshura.
